items.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012
items.q: I was talking in the street with Marc Black who is the musician that Warren was talking about who plays so loud sometimes.

ctx.x: I think I did. LeRoi Jones?

No, no, no, no, no. It’s a Marxist historian. It’s a very interesting book. It’s about music and social change and I found it a fascinating book when I read it. And I also think that if you look at the arts, I think everything is interconnected. I think that World War II, there was an innocence pre-World War II. World War II came, with the advent of the bomb, and with a sense all of us made for the first time that we could face extinction. That gave rise to a different form of literature, the existentialist…

partially because France was a colonial power. And they had a percent of African music in their DNA almost, let alone within their culture. So they saw black musicians as a carrier of a tradition from Africa, whereas America looked at black musicians as, what was jazz, this was like a sexual act. It was like lowbrow music. It was — oh it doesn’t qualify — all the rants against jazz will deprave you, it’ll make your children depraved, and all that stuff. But in France they recognized this music as an offshoot to…
